summary: Defines lightweight versions of IGMPv3 and MLDv2, the protocols hosts use to join multicast groups, that simplify the full versions. It also considers how they interoperate with the full and older versions. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a simpler way for a device to raise its hand and say it wants to hear a group broadcast, with fewer steps than the full process.

questions: how does lw-igmpv3 differ from igmpv3
subtitle: A trimmed-down IGMPv3 and MLDv2 that drops the option to block specific sources.

tldr.problem: Full IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let hosts both include and exclude sources, which makes router state and the rules for updating it complex, even though applications rarely exclude sources.
tldr.mechanism: LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2 keep INCLUDE source lists and the plain (*,G) join, but drop EXCLUDE with a non-empty source list. Routers then no longer track a filter-mode and keep only a group timer and source records.
tldr.outcome: The lightweight versions are subsets of the full ones, use the same message formats and interoperate with them and with IGMPv1/v2 and MLDv1.

facts.label: Router state
facts.value: multicast address, group timer, source records

today: RFC 5790 is a Proposed Standard from February 2010. No obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it, and it builds on RFC 3376 and RFC 3810.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight Version
sections.content:
IGMPv3 and MLDv2 add source filtering to the older IGMPv1, IGMPv2 and MLDv1. A host can tell its router which group it wants to join and which sources it does or does not want to hear from, using INCLUDE and EXCLUDE filter-modes. Routers keep matching filter-modes, group timers and source timers, and with all these factors affecting each other the rules become relatively complex.

The RFC argues that practical applications rarely use EXCLUDE to block sources. A user usually names the sources they want, not the ones they refuse. Even if one user refuses a source, traffic is still forwarded to the shared network when other users want it. So the RFC proposes LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2: subsets that support both Any-Source Multicast (ASM) and Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) without the source-blocking filter.

Because they are subsets, hosts and routers that implement the full versions do not need to change anything to work with lightweight ones.
sections.eli5: Most people only say which shows they want to watch, not which ones to skip. So this version drops the "skip this one" feature and gets simpler.

sections.title: Join Types and Terms
sections.content:
The RFC names several kinds of join:

  • (*,G) join: a host wants group G from all sources. This is typical of ASM.
  • (S,G) join (the same as INCLUDE (S,G) join): a host wants group G only from source S.
  • EXCLUDE (*,G) join: same meaning as a (*,G) join.
  • EXCLUDE (S,G) join: a host wants G but not from source S. This is the one operation that LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2 do not support.

The design principle is to simplify host and router behavior as much as possible while keeping interoperability with the full versions and causing no side effects for applications. The RFC mostly discusses IGMPv3 and notes where MLDv2 differs, since MLDv2 inherits the same source filtering mechanism.
sections.eli5: You can say "I want everything from this channel" or "I want only this one show". You can no longer say "everything except that show".

sections.title: Host Behavior
sections.content:
Hosts keep the same service interface as IGMPv3. INCLUDE mode works as before, while EXCLUDE mode is kept only for an empty source list, which stands for a (*,G) join as used by IGMPv2, IGMPv1 and MLDv1. Query and Report messages are unchanged, and the query response delay rules are inherited from the full version.

What shrinks is the set of group record types. The Current-State types IS_IN and IS_EX are not needed in new reports. A query response for INCLUDE (x,G) uses ALLOW(x), and a response for a (*,G) join uses TO_EX({}). The four types a lightweight host uses are ALLOW, BLOCK, TO_IN and TO_EX. Sending IS_EX({}) or IS_IN(x) in query responses is not prohibited, because routers treat them the same way.

The state-change report table is also short. For example, going from INCLUDE (A) to INCLUDE (B) sends ALLOW(B-A) and BLOCK(A-B), and going from INCLUDE (A) to EXCLUDE ({}) sends TO_EX({}). As in the full version, a state-change report is retransmitted [Robustness Variable]-1 more times.

Example from the RFC: a host runs AP1, which wants INCLUDE (x,G), and sends ALLOW(x). It then runs AP2, which wants (*,G), and sends TO_EX({}). When AP2 ends while AP1 keeps running, the host sends TO_IN(x) for [Robustness Variable] times.
sections.eli5: The host now needs fewer kinds of messages. It can say "add this show", "remove this show", "only these shows" and "everything".

sections.title: Router State and Timers
sections.content:
Routers drop the filter-mode. A lightweight router keeps just (multicast address, group timer, (source records)). The group timer now stands for a (*,G) join. When it is above zero, the router forwards for all sources in the group. When it reaches zero, there are no more (*,G) listeners, so the router keeps only the sources whose source timers are still running, and deletes the group record if none remain.

Source records are also handled more simply. In the full version a source record under EXCLUDE mode is kept until the group timer expires. In the lightweight version there is no need to keep records that block sources, so a source record is deleted as soon as its timer expires.

Forwarding follows directly. With G_Timer above zero the router suggests forwarding. With G_Timer at zero it suggests forwarding from a source only while that source's timer is above zero.

For incoming reports, IS_IN(B) adds B to the source list with timers set to GMI, and IS_EX({}) resets the group timer to GMI. In the same way, ALLOW(B) adds sources, BLOCK(B) sends a query Q(G,A*B), and TO_IN(B) adds sources and queries A-B (plus a query Q(G) if the group timer is running). A router should still process as many messages as it can. If it gets IS_EX(x) or TO_EX(x) with a non-empty list, it treats them as having an empty list.
sections.eli5: The router keeps one note saying whether anybody wants everything, plus a list of individual shows with a timer each. When a timer runs out, that line is crossed off.

sections.title: Interoperability
sections.content:
Lightweight hosts and routers MUST interoperate with the full IGMPv3/MLDv2 and gracefully with IGMPv1/v2 and MLDv1. The message formats do not change. A lightweight host sets its Host Compatibility Mode to IGMPv3 and sends a subset of IGMPv3 reports that full or lightweight routers can read.

A lightweight router MUST translate IS_EX(x) and TO_EX(x) reports from full-version hosts into IS_EX({}) and TO_EX({}). With older versions it behaves like a full IGMPv3 router, using Group Compatibility Mode per group. It maps an IGMPv2 Report to TO_EX({}) and an IGMPv2 Leave to TO_IN({}). An IGMPv1 Report also maps to TO_EX({}). For MLDv1, a Report maps to TO_EX({}) and a Done to TO_IN({}).

Hosts may allow their reports to be suppressed by IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 reports, but since sending older-version packets reduces the capability of the system, the use of backward compatibility may be made configurable.
sections.eli5: The simple version can still talk to old devices and to the full version. It just translates what they say into its own few words.

sections.title: Implementation Notes and Security
sections.content:
The lightweight protocols need no extra procedures for IGMP/MLD snooping, multicast routing protocols or application sockets, while the load on switches and routers running IGMPv3/MLDv2 may be greatly decreased.

For SSM, the rules of RFC 4604 apply, adjusted for the changed message types. A host should not send (*,G) join (TO_EX({})) or (*,G) leave (TO_IN({})) for addresses in the SSM range. A router MUST NOT establish forwarding state on receiving them, and MAY log an error. For the Multicast Source Filter APIs, an LW-IGMPv3 host should implement either the IPv4 Basic or the Protocol-Independent Basic API, and an LW-MLDv2 host the Protocol-Independent Basic API. The Advanced APIs are optional.

The security considerations are the same as those of the full IGMPv3/MLDv2.
sections.eli5: Because the simple version asks less of the machines, they have less work to do. It is as safe, and as unsafe, as the full version.
